seo.metaDescription: Hurt on the job in Calistoga? Get a free case review from an attorney who handles work injury and third-party claims in Napa County.

hero.subtitle: When a job injury sidelines you in Calistoga, the paperwork and rules around workers' comp can feel like a second obstacle on top of recovering. We can help you sort out whether comp or a separate claim fits your situation, at no cost to you.

about.title: Calistoga Workplace Injury Claims
about.longDescription: Calistoga's economy runs on hospitality, agriculture, and the wineries that draw visitors along Lincoln Avenue and out toward Foothill Boulevard, and that mix means work injuries here range from vineyard equipment accidents to kitchen burns to falls at a resort loading dock. California generally routes these injuries through workers' compensation regardless of who was at fault, but that system doesn't always cover everything you've lost, and it isn't the only path available. If a subcontractor, equipment manufacturer, property owner, or another company's employee contributed to what happened, a separate claim against that third party may be possible alongside your workers' comp benefits. We handle workplace injury and third-party claims in Napa County and can explain your options plainly. There's no fee unless a recovery is made.
commonInjuries: Back and spinal strain from lifting or repetitive tasks
Falls from ladders, docks, or uneven vineyard terrain
Burns from kitchen or winery equipment
Crush or laceration injuries from machinery
Heat-related illness during outdoor harvest work
Injuries from forklifts, tractors, or other work vehicles

whyChoose.title: Why Talk to an Attorney First

items.title: Workers' Comp Isn't Always the Whole Story
items.desc: Workers' compensation is usually the exclusive remedy against your employer, but a negligent third party — like a contractor or equipment maker — can still be pursued separately. We can help determine if that applies to your case.

items.title: Reporting Deadlines Move Fast
items.desc: California requires injuries to be reported to your employer within 30 days, and missing that window can complicate your claim. Getting guidance early helps protect your options.

items.title: Retaliation Is Against the Law
items.desc: It's illegal for an employer to punish you for reporting a workplace injury or filing a claim. We can help you understand your rights if you're worried about your job.

items.question: I was hurt at a Calistoga vineyard — do I file workers' comp or a lawsuit?
items.answer: In most cases, workers' compensation is the exclusive remedy against your employer no matter who was at fault. But if equipment failure or a third-party contractor played a role, a separate claim against that party may also be possible. We can review the details and explain which paths apply.

items.question: How long do I have to report a work injury in California?
items.answer: Generally, you need to notify your employer within 30 days of the injury to preserve your workers' comp rights. If a third-party claim is also involved, that carries its own two-year deadline. Acting sooner rather than later helps avoid complications.

items.question: Can my employer fire me for filing a workers' comp claim?
items.answer: No — retaliating against an employee for reporting a workplace injury or filing a claim is illegal in California. If you're facing pressure or pushback at work after an injury, it's worth speaking with us about your options.
